title: What courts actually do
subtitle: American and Scandinavian legal realism
objectives: Explain Holmes's 'bad man' theory and the realist claim that law is best understood as a prediction of what courts will do
Distinguish American rule- and fact-scepticism (Llewellyn, Frank) from Scandinavian realism's metaphysical attack on legal concepts (Olivecrona, Ross)
Apply realist method to a concrete scenario, and state the main objections to realism as a complete account of law

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This lesson doesn't ask you to decide whether the realists were right — it asks whether you can state their strongest case, attack it, and defend it, for both the American and Scandinavian strands. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can name Holmes and Ross — this lesson checks whether you can apply their method to a fact pattern you haven't seen before.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans into scenario-based questions — expect to apply realist reasoning to new facts, not just define it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take your time distinguishing the American and Scandinavian strands before Part 4 asks you to compare them directly.

overview.hook: A judge is deciding a hard case. Ask her why she ruled the way she did, and she'll cite a rule, a precedent, a principle. Ask an American legal realist what actually happened, and you'll get a very different story — one about intuition, temperament, and a rule invoked afterwards to justify a conclusion already reached. Ask a Scandinavian realist a stranger question still: does 'ownership' name anything real at all, or is it a word left over from an age that believed rituals could bind the world? This lesson takes both challenges seriously, and tests how much of formal legal reasoning survives them.

parts.heading: The bad man and the path of the law
parts.voice: argumentative — states Holmes's provocation before drawing out its implications
body: In 1897, Oliver Wendell Holmes opened a lecture to law students with a challenge that still unsettles first-year lawyers: stop asking what the law 'really' requires as a matter of logic or morality, and start asking what courts will, in fact, do.

Holmes's device for making the point was the 'bad man' — a person who cares nothing for ethics, conscience or the 'vaguer sanctions of conscience', and wants to know only one thing: what will happen to him, in practice, if he does X. Study law from that vantage point, Holmes argued, and the moralised vocabulary lawyers use — 'duty', 'right', 'obligation' — dissolves into something much plainer: a prediction of when the public force of the state, acting through the courts, will actually be brought to bear.

This is not a claim that morality is unimportant to law, or that judges shouldn't care about justice. It is a claim about what the discipline of legal science should study if it wants clear, testable answers rather than question-begging appeals to logic dressed up as inevitability. Holmes's famous line captures the target precisely: 'The life of the law has not been logic; it has been experience.'

components.definition: Holmes's analytic device: a person indifferent to morality who wants only a prediction of what courts will actually do to him. Studying law through this lens strips away moralised legal vocabulary and reframes 'law' as a prophecy of official action backed by public force.

interaction.prompt: According to Holmes's 'bad man' theory, what question is a lawyer really answering when they say 'this is legal'?
options: What will a court, as a matter of fact, actually do about it
What does morality require in this situation
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The bad man cares nothing for ethics — only for a prediction of the courts' actual response. That reframing is the whole engine of Holmes's argument.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — the bad man is indifferent to morality by design. Holmes's point is that 'law', studied scientifically, is a prediction of official action, not a statement of what conscience demands.

parts.heading: Rule scepticism and fact scepticism: Llewellyn and Frank
parts.voice: structural — separates two strands of American realism that are often run together
body: Karl Llewellyn's 1931 article 'Some Realism About Realism' is best read as a manifesto that resists being turned into a single doctrine. Llewellyn insisted realism was a method, not a philosophy: a loose family of scholars united by a shared scepticism about how confidently traditional legal scholarship described what courts actually do.

The central working distinction is between 'paper rules' — the rules stated in statutes, textbooks and judgments — and 'real rules', the patterns that actually predict outcomes once you look past what courts say to what they do. Realists like Llewellyn didn't claim rules were meaningless; they claimed the profession routinely overestimated how much of a judge's reasoning the stated rule actually explains.

Jerome Frank pushed a sharper version of this in Law and the Modern Mind (1930): fact-scepticism. Frank argued that even where a rule is perfectly clear, outcomes remain unpredictable because trial-level fact-finding is shot through with the psychology, prejudice and idiosyncrasy of judges and juries. His deeper claim was almost psychoanalytic: the demand for certain, rule-bound law is an infantile wish for a father-figure's fixed authority, and mature legal thought has to accept irreducible uncertainty instead.

components.label: Realism's common working assumptions (Llewellyn, 1931)
points: Law is in flux, and courts constantly remake it in the course of deciding cases
Law is a means to social ends, not an end in itself — its rules should be judged by their effects
Society changes faster than law, so legal rules always need re-examination against current facts
'Paper rules' (what the books say) are routinely distinct from 'real rules' (what courts actually do)
Traditional legal rules, taken alone, are an unreliable guide to how a court will in fact decide a case

components.definition: Rule scepticism (associated with Llewellyn) doubts that stated legal rules reliably predict outcomes. Fact scepticism (associated with Frank) goes further, doubting that even a clear rule produces predictable results, because the fact-finding process itself is unpredictable.

interaction.prompt: In this passage adapted from Llewellyn's 'Some Realism About Realism', highlight the sentence that states the realist's core complaint about how rules are usually studied.
interaction.passage: Lawyers are trained to treat the rules stated in the books as though they were the thing itself. But the rules on paper are important chiefly so far as they help predict what courts will actually do, or help persuade a court to do something — that is their whole importance, beyond their value as objects of professional study in their own right.
interaction.ratioSentence: But the rules on paper are important chiefly so far as they help predict what courts will actually do, or help persuade a court to do something
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the rule-sceptical core: paper rules matter only instrumentally, as evidence for predicting or shaping what courts do — not as a self-sufficient description of the law.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the sentence that reduces the value of stated rules to their predictive or persuasive use, rather than treating them as the law itself.

parts.heading: Crossing the North Sea: Scandinavian realism's attack on legal concepts
parts.voice: philosophical — works outward from the target concept
body: Scandinavian realism, rooted in the Uppsala school of philosophy, is a different animal from its American cousin. It shares the anti-formalist, anti-metaphysical instinct, but its target isn't judicial psychology — it's the reality of legal concepts themselves.

Karl Olivecrona argued that legal rules function as 'independent imperatives': command-like statements that shape behaviour through psychological conditioning built up since childhood, without there being any actual commander whose command they express. A statute reading 'a contract-breaker shall pay damages' feels binding not because some metaphysical bond attaches the breacher to the payment, but because generations of legal education and social practice have conditioned people to respond to that form of words as though it carries binding force.

Alf Ross went further still, treating terms like 'ownership', 'right' and 'validity' as devoid of independent reference. In his later analysis, such words work like his invented example 'tû-tû' — a meaningless intermediate term that simply signals: when certain facts occur (a valid sale, say), treat certain legal consequences as following (the buyer can sue for the goods). On this view, to say a rule of law is 'valid' just is to predict, with reasonable confidence, that courts will apply it — dressed in emotive language inherited from an older belief in a real binding force that, on Ross's account, was never actually there.

components.citation: Ross, On Law and Justice (1953; trans. 1958), paraphrased
components.text: To assert that a rule of law is 'valid' is, properly analysed, nothing more than a prediction that it will, with reasonable probability, be applied by the courts — expressed in an emotively coloured vocabulary inherited from an older idea of an objectively binding force which does not, in fact, exist.
elements: Legal 'validity' is reframed as a predictive, verifiable claim about court behaviour
The emotive language of 'binding force' is inherited, not descriptive of any real entity
This mirrors Holmes's prediction theory, but is reached through a philosophical attack on legal concepts rather than a study of judicial psychology

interaction.prompt: A first-year student insists: 'The company really owns the building — ownership is a genuine relation between the company and the building, not just a label.' Applying Olivecrona and Ross's critique, how would a Scandinavian realist respond?
options: 'Ownership' names no independent reality; it is a linguistic device connecting certain triggering facts (registration, purchase) to certain legal consequences (the power to exclude others), nothing more
The student is correct — ownership is a physical bond comparable to gravity
Scandinavian realists would agree, but only for land, not buildings
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. This is the heart of the Scandinavian critique — legal concepts like ownership are treated as devoid of independent reference, functioning only as shorthand linking facts to consequences.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The Scandinavian move denies that 'ownership' refers to anything real at all — it treats the word as a convenient label connecting a set of facts to a set of legal consequences, not as naming an actual relation.

parts.heading: Two realisms compared
parts.voice: comparative — puts the two strands side by side without collapsing them into one
body: American and Scandinavian realism share real common ground: both reject formal, rule-bound conceptualism; both insist law be studied empirically, as a matter of what actually happens, rather than through logical deduction from stated premises; both grew out of a wider early-twentieth-century turn toward empiricism and pragmatism in the social sciences.

But they diverge sharply in what they're sceptical about. American realism (Holmes, Llewellyn, Frank) is chiefly sceptical about the predictive value of stated rules and about judicial psychology — its home discipline is closer to sociology and behavioural prediction. Scandinavian realism (Olivecrona, Ross), rooted in Hägerström's logical-empiricist philosophy at Uppsala, is chiefly sceptical about the ontological status of legal concepts themselves — its home discipline is closer to philosophy of language and metaphysics.

A useful test: if an argument is about what courts will actually decide, or about the gap between the book-rule and the real pattern of decisions, it's the American strand. If an argument is about whether a legal concept like 'right' or 'duty' refers to anything real at all, it's the Scandinavian strand.

components.title: Classifying a realist claim
components.description: A quick test for sorting an argument into the American or Scandinavian strand of realism.

nodes.label: Is the claim about what courts will actually do, or the gap between stated rules and real patterns of decision?
Yes → American realism (Holmes's prediction theory, Llewellyn's rule scepticism, Frank's fact scepticism)
No → does it deny that a legal concept (right, duty, ownership, validity) refers to anything real?
Yes → Scandinavian realism (Olivecrona's independent imperatives, Ross's tû-tû critique)
Neither → probably not a realist claim at all

components.textAlternative: To classify a realist claim: first ask whether it is about what courts will actually do, or the gap between stated and real rules — if so, it belongs to American realism. If not, ask whether it denies that a legal concept like right, duty or ownership refers to anything real — if so, it belongs to Scandinavian realism. If neither, it likely isn't a realist claim at all.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario best reflects the distinctively Scandinavian, rather than American, strand of legal realism?
interaction.scenarioA: A scholar argues that 'ownership' is a linguistic device with no independent existence — merely a shorthand connecting a set of triggering facts to a set of legal consequences, and that lawyers are mistaken to think it names any real relation between a person and a thing.
interaction.scenarioB: A scholar argues that studying what appellate courts have actually decided in the last 200 negligence cases is a better guide to how the next case will be decided than reciting the textbook formula for the duty of care.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. A attacks the reality of the legal concept itself — the Scandinavian move. B is an empirical, behavioural claim about predicting judicial outcomes — the American move.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what each scholar is sceptical of. A denies a legal concept refers to anything real (Scandinavian); B is about predicting what courts will actually do (American) — without denying that 'duty of care' refers to anything.

parts.heading: What realism leaves unexplained
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the standard objection before answering it
body: Realism's most influential critic is H. L. A. Hart, and his objection cuts at both strands. If law really is nothing but a prediction of official behaviour, how do we explain the fact that judges, officials and citizens experience rules as genuinely binding — as reasons for acting, not just as reliable forecasts of what will happen to them? Hart called this the 'internal point of view', and argued realism, taken to its extreme, cannot account for it: prediction theories describe how an outside observer sees the system, not how participants inside it actually reason.

Hart also pushed back against overclaiming indeterminacy. Most rules, he argued, have a 'core of settled meaning' where application is genuinely straightforward — a 'no vehicles in the park' rule plainly excludes a car, whatever penumbral disputes it generates about bicycles or skateboards. Realists who treat every legal question as radically open risk exaggerating the uncertainty that actually exists.

None of this defeats realism outright — it remains a powerful corrective against naive formalism, and it seeded an entire empirical tradition (the sociology of law, and later the law-and-economics movement covered in Lesson 12) that studies what legal rules actually do rather than assuming the text settles everything. The fair conclusion is narrower: realism explains a great deal about legal uncertainty and judicial behaviour, but struggles, on its own, to explain why law feels normative — like something people are bound by, not merely something that happens to them.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often summarise American realism as the claim that judicial decisions are essentially random, or determined by 'what the judge had for breakfast'.
components.whyItsWrong: That's a caricature. Realists like Llewellyn explicitly claimed that patterns exist and can be studied empirically — their point was that the real pattern often diverges from the stated rule, not that no pattern exists at all. Frank's fact-scepticism goes further than Llewellyn, but even Frank was describing systematic sources of unpredictability (fact-finding psychology), not pure randomness.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that American legal realism denies any predictable pattern exists in judicial decision-making (the 'breakfast' caricature)?
sliderLabels: Realism denies any predictable pattern exists
Realism claims patterns exist and can be studied empirically
interaction.explanation: Realists claimed the real pattern of decisions often diverges from the stated 'paper rule' — not that decisions are random. Llewellyn's whole programme depends on patterns being real and discoverable through empirical study.

testPool.prompt: State Holmes's 'bad man' theory of what law is.
acceptableAnswers: law is a prediction of what courts will do
look at law through the eyes of someone who cares only about consequences, not morals
testPool.modelAnswer: Holmes said that to see the law clearly, we should study it through the eyes of the 'bad man', who cares nothing for ethics but wants to know what courts will in fact do — law, on this view, is simply a prediction of the incidence of public force through the courts.

testPool.prompt: Which phrase did Llewellyn use to distinguish the rules stated in statutes and textbooks from what courts actually do?
Which of the following is NOT a claim made by American legal realists?
options: Judicial decisions can be predicted more accurately by studying what courts do than by studying formal rules alone
Law should be evaluated in terms of its actual social effects
Legal concepts like 'right' and 'duty' correspond to no reality and are essentially magical survivals from primitive belief
'Paper rules' often diverge from the 'real rules' courts actually apply
testPool.trapExplanation: That metaphysical attack on legal concepts as empty of real reference is the Scandinavian realists' contribution (Olivecrona, Ross), not the American realists', who focused on judicial behaviour and prediction rather than the ontology of legal language.

Properly analysed, however, this is nothing more than a confident prediction that the rule will be applied by the courts, dressed in emotive language inherited from an older, and mistaken, belief in a real binding force.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that reflects a realist, prediction-based style of legal advice.
testPool.scenarioText: A junior associate is advising a client on the strength of a contested employment tribunal claim. She reads the leading statute and textbook commentary, then adds: 'But this particular tribunal panel has ruled against employers in near-identical claims four times running over the past two years — that's what will actually decide it.'
tappableSpans: reads the leading statute and textbook commentary
this particular tribunal panel has ruled against employers in near-identical claims four times running
that's what will actually decide it
testPool.correctSpan: that's what will actually decide it
testPool.explanation: That's the realist move in miniature — treating the pattern of what the tribunal has actually done as the real basis for prediction, over and above what the statute and textbooks say the law 'is'.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario best reflects the distinctively Scandinavian, rather than American, strand of legal realism?
testPool.scenarioA: A scholar argues 'ownership' is a linguistic fiction connecting certain facts to certain consequences, with no independent reality behind the word at all.
testPool.scenarioB: A scholar argues that studying a court's actual pattern of past decisions predicts its next ruling better than reciting the formal legal test.
testPool.explanation: A is the Scandinavian move — an attack on the reality of legal concepts themselves. B is the American realist move — an empirical, behavioural focus on predicting what courts will actually do.

testPool.prompt: Applying Holmes's 'bad man' theory, which question is the correct one to ask when advising a manufacturer on whether it 'must' fit a safety guard to a machine?
options: What does the abstract moral duty of care require?
What, in practice, will a court do to the company if it doesn't fit one and someone is hurt?
What would a reasonable person consider fair?
testPool.explanation: The bad man theory asks not what morality demands but what courts will, as a matter of fact, do to you — the prediction of official action, not the moral quality of the duty, is what 'law' means on this view.

testPool.prompt: A small business is told by its solicitor that 'the law clearly requires' 28 days' notice before terminating a commercial lease, but a realist-minded colleague points out that the local county court has, in the last six comparable cases, accepted much shorter notice as sufficient whenever the tenant had already vacated. Using realist method, analyse how a lawyer applying Holmesian/Llewellyn-style reasoning would advise the client, as against a lawyer relying purely on the textbook rule.
factsToOrder: The textbook states a clear 28-day notice rule
The local county court has departed from that rule in six recent comparable cases
The tenant in this case has already vacated the premises
The client wants a reliable prediction of the practical outcome, not a restatement of the formal rule

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the client should be advised according to the textbook's stated notice rule or according to the pattern of what the local court has actually done in comparable cases.
modelAnswer.rule: Realist method (Holmes, Llewellyn) treats 'law' as a prediction of what courts will in fact do, and distinguishes 'paper rules' from the 'real rules' revealed by a court's actual pattern of decisions; where the two diverge, the realist advises according to the pattern of practice, not the formal text.
modelAnswer.application: The textbook's 28-day rule is a paper rule. The real rule, evidenced by six recent comparable decisions accepting shorter notice once the tenant has vacated, better predicts what this court will actually do — and the tenant here has already vacated, which is the fact pattern the court has treated as decisive.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A realist-minded lawyer would advise the client that, on the pattern of recent decisions, a shorter notice period is likely to be accepted by this court, notwithstanding the textbook's 28-day statement — while flagging that this is a prediction, not a guarantee.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this exchange that reflects Scandinavian realism's attack on legal concepts, rather than the American realists' focus on judicial behaviour.
testPool.scenarioText: A first-year student says: 'I used to think "I own this car" described a real bond between me and the car. Now I think "ownership" is just legal shorthand — when certain facts occur, like buying it, courts treat a certain set of legal consequences as following, and "ownership" just labels that whole facts-to-consequences package, with nothing more behind it.'
tappableSpans: a real bond between me and the car
testPool.explanation: That's the Scandinavian move precisely — denying that a concept like 'ownership' names any independent reality beyond the rule connecting facts to consequences, echoing Ross's tû-tû critique and Olivecrona's attack on legal concepts as empty of real referents.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps in Olivecrona's account of how a legal imperative influences behaviour without any actual commander behind it.
items: A rule is announced in the form of an imperative (e.g. 'a contract-breaker shall pay damages')
Citizens are conditioned, from childhood and through legal education, to associate this form of words with a felt sense of being bound
The rule shapes behaviour through this psychological conditioning, not because any actual sovereign commands it
Officials and citizens experience the rule as 'binding', though Olivecrona denies any real binding force exists

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake here is treating 'realism' as one undifferentiated attack on formalism. American realism is chiefly about predicting judicial behaviour; Scandinavian realism is chiefly about denying legal concepts refer to anything real. Keep the two separate.
